claims.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi' that covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
Debugging AWS CDK was frustrating because of CloudFormation templates obscuring underlying logic.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allowed developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.

AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator, producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code the developer writes is not the code running during deployment.
AWS CDK supports only AWS, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployment is slower than Pulumi because of CloudFormation, while Pulumi has faster direct execution.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK uses a CloudFormation state file while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
With AWS CDK, secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem while Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, the SST team often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployment.
Pulumi Insights (linked product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments provides advanced deployment workflows, such as faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and granular control over the deployment process.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console.
SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your infrastructure easy.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account, not in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 has no Pulumi Cloud dependency, and does not use CDK or CloudFormation.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
SST's team is also behind opencode, an AI coding agent.
The SST team has repeatedly said, since the rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs page "What is SST" states: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis" states: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka's article "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion" states: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The `platform/package.json` lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The SST repository lives at `anomalyco/sst`, formerly `sst/sst`.
In SST's deploy chain, SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations, and the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge translates each resource into cloud API calls via Terraform-bridged providers.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, in the same embedded fashion.
Pulumi's provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.

Cross-references: Automation API docs (/docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/), /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/, /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/ must exist.
Nitric's docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose official providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider README describes taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly with Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app, because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
opencode is an open source AI coding agent that now has a larger GitHub star count than SST itself.
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode, and SST's release cadence is unchanged.
If you run SST you are already running Pulumi's engine, whether or not you have written Pulumi code.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides centrally enforced guardrails, and Pulumi components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization; none require leaving the engine SST already uses.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework where infrastructure and code are defined together.
